title: Berger and the EEG
text:
CHAPTER 10. RECORDING THE LIVING BRAIN
SECTION 10.1. BERGER AND THE EEG

Listening to the whole brain

The methods we have met so far record from single cells or small structures: an electrode inside a squid axon, a microelectrode next to a neuron in a cat's visual cortex, a patch pipette sealed to a membrane. These methods are precise, but they are invasive and look at a tiny part of the brain at a time. Is it possible to record the activity of the human brain from outside the head, without surgery? The answer, discovered in the early twentieth century, is yes, by recording the small voltages that brain activity produces on the scalp. This is electroencephalography, or EEG. It remains one of the most widely used tools in neuroscience and medicine, and it is the basis of many non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.

Before Berger: Caton and Beck

The first recordings of the brain's electrical activity were made in animals. In 1875, Richard Caton, a physician in Liverpool, reported to the British Medical Association that he had detected feeble electrical currents from the exposed brains of rabbits and monkeys using a sensitive galvanometer. He observed that these currents fluctuated continuously and that they changed when the animal was stimulated, for example when light was shone into its eyes, with changes in the region of cortex associated with vision. In 1890, Adolf Beck, a Polish physiologist, independently reported spontaneous electrical oscillations in the brains of dogs and rabbits, and showed that these oscillations were suppressed by sensory stimulation, a phenomenon now called desynchronization. Other researchers, such as Vladimir Pravdich-Neminsky in Russia, published early photographic recordings of brain activity in dogs in the 1910s.

Hans Berger

Hans Berger (1873 to 1941) was a German psychiatrist at the University of Jena. As a young man he reportedly had an experience that convinced him of the possibility of telepathy: he fell from a horse during military service and was nearly run over, and on that same day his sister, far away, sent a telegram expressing worry about him. Berger's later writings suggest that he was motivated by a desire to understand "psychic energy" and the relationship between brain and mind. Whatever his motivations, he worked for many years, largely in secret, trying to detect electrical activity from the human brain.

In 1924, Berger succeeded in recording electrical oscillations from the scalp of a human subject. His first recordings were from patients with skull defects (areas where bone was missing after surgery), where the electrodes could be closer to the brain, and later from intact heads, including his son Klaus. After years of checking that the signals were not artifacts from muscles, the heart, or the skin, he published his first paper, "Uber das Elektrenkephalogramm des Menschen" ("On the electroencephalogram of man"), in 1929. He introduced the term electroencephalogram (German Elektrenkephalogramm).

Berger described two main types of waves:

- Alpha waves: relatively large, regular oscillations at about 10 cycles per second, most prominent when the subject was awake and relaxed with eyes closed, and best recorded over the back of the head. When the subject opened the eyes or performed mental arithmetic, the alpha waves were reduced or disappeared ("alpha blocking").
- Beta waves: smaller, faster oscillations that appeared when alpha was blocked, during alertness or mental effort.

Berger's work was initially met with skepticism, partly because the signals were tiny (tens of microvolts) and the risk of artifacts was high, and partly because Berger was not well known in physiology. The turning point came in 1934, when Edgar Adrian and Bryan Matthews in Cambridge replicated and confirmed his findings, including alpha blocking. Adrian, already a Nobel laureate (section 4.2), gave the alpha rhythm the name "Berger rhythm" in his honor. After that, EEG research spread rapidly. Berger's later years were difficult; he was forced into retirement in 1938 under the Nazi regime, though the circumstances and his own political positions have been discussed by historians, and he died by suicide in 1941.

What does EEG measure?

The EEG records voltage differences between electrodes on the scalp. These voltages are produced mainly by the synchronized synaptic activity of large populations of cortical pyramidal neurons. Here is the physical picture.

Pyramidal neurons in the cortex are arranged in parallel, with their long apical dendrites pointing toward the cortical surface. When many synapses on these dendrites are activated, current flows into the dendrites at the synapses (a "sink" in the extracellular space) and out of the cell elsewhere (a "source"). This creates a small current dipole: a separation of positive and negative regions in the extracellular fluid. A single neuron's dipole is far too weak to detect at the scalp. But when tens of thousands or millions of aligned pyramidal neurons receive synchronous input, their dipoles add up, producing a field strong enough to be measured through the cerebrospinal fluid, skull, and scalp.

Several consequences follow:

- EEG mainly reflects synaptic currents (postsynaptic potentials), not action potentials. Action potentials are brief (about a millisecond), and their currents tend to cancel because of their shape and timing; synaptic potentials last longer (tens of milliseconds) and summate better.
- EEG mainly reflects activity in the cortex, especially in neurons oriented perpendicular to the scalp (on the crowns of gyri). Deeper structures contribute less.
- EEG requires synchrony. If neurons are active but out of phase, their contributions cancel. So EEG is sensitive to rhythmic, coordinated activity and relatively insensitive to unsynchronized activity.
- Spatial resolution is poor. The skull is a poor conductor and smears the electrical field over the scalp (volume conduction), so each electrode picks up activity from a wide area, on the order of several square centimeters of cortex or more. Localizing the sources of EEG signals inside the brain is an ill-posed "inverse problem": many different arrangements of sources can produce the same scalp pattern, and additional assumptions are needed to find a unique solution.
- Temporal resolution is excellent, on the order of milliseconds, because electrical fields propagate essentially instantaneously.

In engineering terms, EEG is a very low-spatial-resolution but high-temporal-resolution sensor of the summed, synchronized current dipoles in the cortex, observed through a conducting volume that acts as a spatial low-pass filter.

Recording practice

Modern EEG uses electrodes, typically silver/silver chloride (section 2.1), placed on the scalp with a conductive gel or saline, at positions defined by the international 10-20 system. This system, proposed by Herbert Jasper in 1958, places electrodes at distances of 10 or 20 percent of the total distance between skull landmarks (the nasion at the bridge of the nose, the inion at the back of the skull, and the preauricular points in front of the ears). Electrodes are named by region (Fp for frontopolar, F frontal, C central, P parietal, O occipital, T temporal) and by number (odd on the left, even on the right, z for midline). Higher-density systems with 64, 128, or 256 electrodes are common in research.

The signals are small (typically 10 to 100 microvolts), so EEG amplifiers must have high gain, high input impedance, and excellent common-mode rejection, since the body picks up mains interference (50 Hz in Mongolia and most of the world, 60 Hz in North America) far larger than the EEG itself. Instrumentation amplifiers, careful grounding, shielding, and notch filters are standard. Artifacts from eye movements and blinks (the eye is an electrical dipole), muscle activity, heartbeat, and electrode movement must be identified and removed, often using signal processing methods such as independent component analysis (ICA), which separates the recorded signals into statistically independent sources.

Brain rhythms

EEG is usually described in terms of frequency bands. Conventional definitions vary somewhat between sources, but typical ranges are:

- Delta: about 0.5 to 4 Hz. Prominent in deep (slow-wave) sleep and in infants; in awake adults, may indicate pathology.
- Theta: about 4 to 8 Hz. Seen in drowsiness and in some memory and navigation tasks (note that the rodent hippocampal theta rhythm of section 9.3 is measured within the brain, and its relationship to human scalp theta is not simple).
- Alpha: about 8 to 12 Hz. Relaxed wakefulness, eyes closed, mostly posterior. A related rhythm over the motor cortex, the mu rhythm, is suppressed by movement and by imagining movement, which is important for brain-computer interfaces (chapter 14).
- Beta: about 13 to 30 Hz. Active thinking, alertness; beta over motor cortex is associated with maintaining a motor state.
- Gamma: roughly 30 to 100 Hz or higher. Associated with active processing and attention, though gamma is difficult to record from the scalp because of muscle artifacts.

The functional roles of these rhythms are the subject of much research and debate. Hypotheses include: alpha as a mechanism of "gating by inhibition," suppressing processing in task-irrelevant regions (proposed by Ole Jensen and Ali Mazaheri, among others); gamma as a signature of local cortical processing, generated by interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons; and coherence between rhythms in different regions as a mechanism for communication between areas (the "communication through coherence" hypothesis of Pascal Fries). Gyorgy Buzsaki's book Rhythms of the Brain (2006) provides an influential overview.

Sleep

EEG revolutionized the study of sleep. In the 1930s, Alfred Loomis, E. Newton Harvey, and Garret Hobart described distinct stages of sleep based on EEG patterns. In 1953, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman at the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep: periods during sleep when the eyes move rapidly, the EEG resembles that of wakefulness, and subjects awakened often report vivid dreams. William Dement, working with Kleitman, described the cycle of sleep stages through the night. Michel Jouvet in France showed that REM sleep is accompanied by muscle paralysis (atonia) and studied its brainstem mechanisms.

Modern sleep scoring, based on EEG, eye movements, and muscle activity (polysomnography), distinguishes wakefulness, non-REM stages N1, N2 (with characteristic sleep spindles and K-complexes), and N3 (slow-wave sleep with large delta waves), and REM sleep. As discussed in section 9.2, slow oscillations, spindles, and hippocampal ripples during non-REM sleep are thought to coordinate memory consolidation.

Clinical uses: epilepsy and beyond

EEG quickly became essential in diagnosing epilepsy. In 1935, Frederic Gibbs, Hallowell Davis, and William Lennox at Harvard described the characteristic "3 per second spike-and-wave" pattern of absence seizures (then called petit mal). EEG can show abnormal discharges between seizures (interictal spikes) that indicate a tendency to seizures and help localize their origin. Long-term video-EEG monitoring is used to characterize seizures and plan surgery. In patients being evaluated for epilepsy surgery, electrodes are sometimes placed directly on or in the brain (electrocorticography, ECoG, or stereo-EEG), giving signals with much higher spatial resolution and bandwidth. These intracranial recordings have also provided rare data on human brain activity for research, including the speech decoding studies discussed in chapter 14.

EEG is also used to monitor depth of anesthesia, to assess coma and brain death (together with other criteria), and to study sleep disorders.

Event-related potentials

Much cognitive neuroscience research uses event-related potentials (ERPs): the average EEG response time-locked to a repeated stimulus or event. Because the brain's response to a single stimulus is small compared with ongoing EEG activity, averaging many trials cancels the activity unrelated to the stimulus and reveals the consistent response. Averaging improves the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of the square root of the number of trials, assuming the noise is independent across trials.

ERPs have characteristic components, named by polarity (P for positive, N for negative) and approximate latency or order. Examples include:

- The P300 (or P3): a positive wave peaking roughly 300 milliseconds or later after an infrequent, task-relevant stimulus (an "oddball"). Described by Samuel Sutton and colleagues in 1965, it is used in the P300 speller, one of the first and most widely studied EEG-based brain-computer interfaces (chapter 14).
- The N400: a negative wave around 400 milliseconds after a word that is semantically unexpected in its context ("I take coffee with cream and dog"). Described by Marta Kutas and Steven Hillyard in 1980, it has been used extensively in language research.
- The mismatch negativity (MMN): a response to a deviant sound in a sequence of repeated sounds, even when the subject is not paying attention, described by Risto Naatanen and colleagues in 1978. It is often interpreted in terms of predictive processing (chapter 13).

MEG

A related technique is magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by the same neural currents that generate EEG. These fields are extremely weak, on the order of femtoteslas to picoteslas, billions of times weaker than the Earth's magnetic field. David Cohen at MIT made the first MEG recordings in 1968 using induction coils in a magnetically shielded room, and in 1972 he used a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), a superconducting sensor developed by James Zimmerman and others, to obtain much clearer recordings. MEG has better spatial localization than EEG for some sources, because magnetic fields are not distorted by the skull, but it requires expensive shielded rooms and cryogenic cooling. Newer optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs), which do not require cryogenics and can be worn on the head, are being developed and could make MEG more practical.

Bridge to AI: EEG, signal processing, and machine learning

EEG is a natural meeting point for neuroscience, signal processing, and machine learning.

Feature extraction and classification. Traditional EEG analysis extracts features such as band power (the energy in the alpha, beta, or other bands, computed by Fourier or wavelet transforms), coherence between channels, or ERP amplitudes, and then uses classifiers to detect patterns, such as seizures, sleep stages, or the user's intentions in a brain-computer interface. Common spatial patterns (CSP), a method that finds spatial filters maximizing the variance difference between two classes, became a standard technique for motor imagery BCIs.

Deep learning. Since the mid-2010s, deep networks have been applied directly to raw or minimally processed EEG. Architectures like EEGNet (Vernon Lawhern and colleagues, 2018), a compact convolutional network designed for EEG, and various recurrent and transformer models have been used for seizure detection, sleep staging, emotion recognition, and BCI decoding. Automatic sleep staging with deep networks has reached agreement with human experts comparable to the agreement between different human experts in some studies. Large "foundation models" for EEG, pretrained on large collections of recordings with self-supervised objectives, are a recent research direction.

Caution. EEG data are noisy, vary greatly between individuals and sessions, and are easy to overfit. Some published claims of decoding complex mental content from EEG (such as images or words) have been criticized for experimental design flaws that allowed classifiers to exploit confounds, such as the order in which stimuli were presented. This is a valuable lesson for any machine learning engineer: a classifier will exploit any reliable signal in the data, including artifacts and confounds, and careful experimental design is essential.

Rhythms in AI. Artificial neural networks generally lack oscillations. But some researchers have explored oscillatory or phase-based computations in neural networks, such as networks of coupled oscillators for binding features together, and "complex-valued" or phase-coding neurons. Whether brain rhythms are essential for computation or mainly side effects of circuit dynamics is still debated in neuroscience, and the answer may inform whether such mechanisms would help AI.

Summary

- Richard Caton (1875) and Adolf Beck (1890) recorded brain electrical activity in animals.
- Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924 and published in 1929, describing alpha and beta waves; Adrian and Matthews confirmed his work in 1934.
- EEG reflects synchronized postsynaptic currents of aligned cortical pyramidal neurons, with excellent temporal resolution but poor spatial resolution; source localization is an ill-posed inverse problem.
- Recording uses the 10-20 system and high-quality differential amplifiers; artifacts are removed with methods like ICA.
- Brain rhythms (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) relate to states and functions; EEG enabled the discovery of REM sleep (1953) and is central to epilepsy diagnosis.
- Event-related potentials (P300, N400, MMN) are obtained by averaging; MEG measures the corresponding magnetic fields.
- EEG analysis increasingly uses machine learning, which demands care to avoid exploiting artifacts and confounds.
